title: Articles: der, die, das, ein, eine
objective: Identify the definite and indefinite article for a noun and understand that gender must be learned with each noun.
explanation: German nouns have one of three grammatical genders: masculine (der/ein), feminine (die/eine), and neuter (das/ein). Unlike Danish, where "en" and "et" give two choices, German has three. The gender of a noun cannot reliably be guessed from the noun's meaning, so you learn each noun together with its article: "der Tisch" (the table, masc.), "die Schule" (the school, fem.), "das Buch" (the book, neut.). In the definite form "das Buch" uses "das"; in the indefinite form it uses "ein Buch" (neuter and masculine share "ein" in the indefinite nominative). This lesson focuses on recognising and matching articles — not on case endings, which come later.
sourceReference: Teacher-authored example. Article forms verified against standard German grammar (nominative definite and indefinite articles, three-gender system).

exercises.prompt: "Buch" (book) is neuter. Which sentence uses the correct definite article?
exercises.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Neuter nouns take "das" as the definite article: "das Buch".
exercises.feedbackIncorrect: "Buch" is neuter. Neuter nouns take "das", not "der" (masculine) or "die" (feminine).

options.text: der Buch liegt auf dem Tisch.
die Buch liegt auf dem Tisch.
das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch.

exercises.prompt: "Schule" (school) is feminine. Complete: "___ Schule ist groß."
exercises.feedbackCorrect: Correct. "Die Schule" — feminine nouns take "die" as the definite article.
exercises.feedbackIncorrect: Feminine nouns take "die". "Die Schule ist groß." — learn the article together with each new noun.

exercises.prompt: Choose three German nouns you know or look up. Write each with its definite article (der/die/das) and then with its indefinite article (ein/eine/ein).
